live.name: MageCart
live.headline: MageCart: a threat actor listed in the MISP galaxy
live.in_short: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue. The record gives no aliases and no tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: MageCart is a threat actor named in the MISP galaxy catalogue.
The catalogue record lists no aliases and no tools for it.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: card-skimming code planted on online checkout pages
next.in_short: MageCart is a name for web skimming: JavaScript slipped onto checkout pages to steal card details. Several groups use it, and reports describe attacks on thousands of sites.

sentences.t: Malpedia describes Magecart as a malware framework meant to steal credit card information from compromised eCommerce websites.
Trend Micro says multiple groups are using the Magecart code, which it describes as a piece of malicious JavaScript.
Headlines in Malpedia's reference list name several groups tied to Magecart activity, including Magecart Groups 4, 8 and 12, FIN6, Mirrorthief and ATMZOW.
eSentire says the FIN7 group is one of many cyber gangs observed taking part in Magecart attacks.
WIRED reports that Magecart hackers cast the widest possible net to find vulnerable ecommerce sites.

Trend Micro lists victims across retail, an airline, ticketing and higher education. These include Newegg, Target, Home Depot, Ticketmaster and online campus stores serving nearly 200 universities in the US and Canada.
A Malpedia reference headline reports campaigns that infected 311 restaurants on online ordering platforms.

ANY.RUN describes one campaign that mostly hit retail e-commerce sites, with victims in at least 12 countries. It says the incidents were concentrated in Spain, France and the United States, and that banks, not merchants, bear the primary impact.
Malpedia says the first stage is typically JavaScript on a compromised checkout page. It relays card data to command-and-control servers.
A report on the Volusion breach says most Magecart attacks start when hackers use vulnerabilities in self-hosted stores to plant skimmer code.

Trend Micro describes attackers infecting third-party companies that supply code to other sites. It also describes automated scans for unsecured servers and skimming code that works across many payment pages.
Malwarebytes reports Magecart-linked skimmers hosted on Heroku. A single injected line of code loads the script, a fake payment frame overlays the real form, and stolen data returns in encoded form.
Sucuri describes the ATMZOW skimmer, which is planted through Google Tag Manager containers. In late 2023 it used heavy obfuscation and 40 newly registered domains, many hidden behind a firewall.
ANY.RUN describes a campaign that hijacked checkout steps, imitated payment pages and sent card data over WebSocket.

RiskIQ reports that a Magecart actor registered a lookalike domain on August 13th and put a skimmer on Newegg's payment page around August 14th. It was removed on September 18th, so customers were exposed for over a month.
RiskIQ says the Newegg skimmer reused code recognisable from the British Airways incident.
In October 2019 hackers breached Volusion, a cloud store provider. The report says more than 6,500 stores were impacted and the number could be higher.
WIRED reported in July 2019 that one Magecart group had hit 17,000 domains in a few months. It named British Airways and Ticketmaster among past hacks.
ANY.RUN says one large campaign stayed active for at least 24 months and was supported by over 100 domains.
Shop owners should review which scripts load on their checkout pages and look into any they do not recognise.
